messages.author: 659179b11b955d52
messages.subject: Multiple time series in R-INLA
parts:
Hello everyone,

I would like to understand the difference between two ways to specify temporal random effects in INLA.
Let’s say we follow 30 subjects over a period of 10 years. 
Every year, we measure some variable Y and we collect some covariates (X1, X2, and X3).
The dataset has of 6 columns: Year, Subject_ID, X1, X2, X3, Y.

If I want to determine the effect of the covariates on Y for each subject while accounting for temporal correlation (which I hypothesize is specific to each individual) should I use:
1) inla( Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + f(Subjects, Year, model = ‘iid’, data = my_data)
as suggested here https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-multilevel.html#multilevel-models-for-longitudinal-data 

2) my_data$ID_subject_1 <- as.numeric(my_data$Subject == 1)
my_data$ID_subject_2 <- as.numeric(my_data$Subject == 2)
|
|
my_data$ID_subject_30 <- as.numeric(my_data$Subject == 30)
inla( Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + f(Year, ID_subject_1, model = ‘rw1’) + f(Year, ID_subject_2, model = ‘rw1’) + … + f(Year, ID_subject_30, model = ‘rw1’) 
as suggested here https://tem11010.github.io/timeseries-inla/

Now, if I want my random effect ‘Subject_ID’ to be nested into a variable ’Site’ but still account for individual autocorrelation in time, is this correct:
Zssub   <- as(model.matrix(~ 0 + site:subject, data = my_data), ‘Matrix’)
my_data$Sub_ID <- 1:nrow(my_data) 
inla( Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + f(Subjects, Year, model = ‘iid’, data = my_data) + f(Sub_ID, model = ‘z’, matrix = Zssub)

I have the feeling that just separating the temporal effect and the multilevel structure does not make any sense. Is there a specific type of model (implemented in INLA) that is capable of handling multilevel time series? Any book/article/tutorial would be much appreciated. 

Thanks,
Camille

messages.author: 936ef8c6d12fc338
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple time series in R-INLA
parts:
Dear Camille,

What I often use is f(Year, model = "rw1", replicate = Subject). That yield a rw1 model for each subject but with common hyperparameters for all subjects.

Best regards,

messages.author: 5063972801d34964
messages.subject: RE: Re: [r-inla] Multiple time series in R-INLA
parts:
Camille:

 

I think all of those could work; it helps to remember that despite these nifty constructs we have come up with for tracking dependence among observations, they are all simplifications of the truth and different ones work better for different data sets, often just because of peculiarities of different problems.  Sometimes it is a matter of resources, in that the “iid” models (either varying intercept or nested) tend to stress INLA less than the other latent variable structures.  Generally speaking it is a good idea to try various different types and see which ones provides the most robust fit for your data.  I think looking for the one “right” way is unlikely to prove fruitful.

 

With that said, what Thierry suggests is a good choice. The “ar1” and “rw2” models also work well in the “replicate” framework for subject-year dependence, and I would try those too.

 

Jonathan

parts:
Hi everyone,

Thank you all for your help. 

Following your advice, I am running different models to test which option yields the best fit, and so far, the « replicate » option seems to work better regarding the CPO and BIC coefficients.
However, it also shows « fails » on the CPO graph which (to my understanding) suggests these data points are most likely outliers (in the context of this specific model). Other models also detect some outliers but not as many as this one. I guess it means that the « replicate » model is better at explaining my data but at the expense of excluding some data points whereas other models are more inclusive but less accurate.

Is there some good practice when dealing with these contradicting results? 
Or is it one of these cases where I should rule between the models based :
- on my knowledge of my data
- eventually, some biological meaning
- my study goal: I am not interested in performing predictions but rather in understand which factors affect my dependent variable.


Thank you everyone,

Camille
